title: Exhaustion of parabolics by simple-root subsets
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $G$ be a reductive $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme, lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]: smooth, connected, affine and of finite type, with no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup. Smoothness, connectedness and finite type mean [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Unipotent means that all geometric points are unipotent matrices in a faithful finite-dimensional representation. Let $T\subseteq G$ be a split maximal torus: a closed subgroup [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup] isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$ for some $r\geq0$, maximal among torus subgroups; $\mathbf G_m$ is [def-sc-gm-ga]. Let $P\subseteq G$ be a smooth connected closed subgroup whose fppf right-coset sheaf $G/P$ is represented by a proper finite-type $F$-scheme [def-weil-proper-morphism]. This sheaf is sheafification of $A\mapsto G(A)/P(A)$ for faithfully flat finitely presented coverings of commutative $F$-algebras, with $G(A)=\operatorname{Hom}_F(\operatorname{Spec}A,G)$. Assume $T\subseteq P$. Let $X=X^*(T)=\operatorname{Hom}_{F\text{-grp}}(T,\mathbf G_m)$, and let $\Phi\subseteq X\setminus\{0\}$ be the characters occurring in the conjugation representation of $T$ on the tangent space $\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ at $1$. Put $\Phi_P=\{\alpha\in\Phi:\operatorname{Lie}(P)_\alpha\ne0\}$, using character-weight spaces, not differentials of characters. Then there exists a Borel subgroup $T\subseteq B\subseteq P$ of $G$. A Borel is a maximal smooth connected solvable closed subgroup, and solvable means that its successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroups become trivial. For every such $B$, let $\Phi^+$ be its positive roots and $\Delta$ their simple-root base as in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]; thus $\Delta$ is linearly independent in $X\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$ and every root has integral $\Delta$-coefficients all nonnegative or all nonpositive. There is a unique subset $I\subseteq\Delta$ such that
$$\Phi_P=\Phi^+\cup(\Phi\cap\mathbf Z I),$$
where $\mathbf Z I$ is the subgroup of $X$ generated by $I$. Equivalently $I=\{\alpha\in\Delta:-\alpha\in\Phi_P\}$. No semisimplicity, simply connectedness or characteristic restriction is imposed; $G=T$, $P=G$ and empty root sets are allowed.

source.place: Theorem 17.16 (printed p.356) and maximal-torus conjugacy in the connected group P, Theorem 17.10 (printed pp.354--355), give B through T; Theorem 21.91 (printed pp.453--454), Proposition 21.90 (printed p.453), and the reductive-to-semisimple quotient reduction at the start of section 21.i (printed p.452) give exhaustion and the displayed root set. The rational independence is the simple-root-base property in section 21.c.

proof.text: Choose a Borel $B_0$ of $G$ using [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. Left multiplication defines its action on the nonempty proper finite-type scheme $G/P$. By [lem-sfb-solvable-proper-fixed-point] there is a scheme-theoretically fixed point $x\in(G/P)(F)$. The represented quotient is the quotient of [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry], by the universal property of fppf sheafification; that node lifts $x$ to $g\in G(F)$. For every $F$-algebra $A$ and $b\in B_0(A)$, fixedness and the quotient's equality-of-cosets criterion give $g^{-1}bg\in P(A)$. Thus the conjugate Borel $B_1=g^{-1}B_0g$ is contained in $P$ as a subgroup scheme.

source.place: Theorem 17.16, printed p.356, converse proof, using Corollary 17.3.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-borel-maximal-torus-conjugacy], $B_1$ contains a torus $S$ maximal in $G$. Both $S$ and the prescribed $T$ are maximal tori of the smooth connected group $P$: any larger torus in $P$ would be a larger torus in $G$. Apply the same node to $P$ to obtain $p\in P(F)$ with $pSp^{-1}=T$. Then $B=pB_1p^{-1}$ is a Borel of $G$, is contained in $P$, and contains $T$. Henceforth fix any Borel with these two containments, not only the one just constructed.

source.place: Theorem 17.10 and paragraph following Definition 17.12, printed pp.354--355, applied inside P after Theorem 17.16.

proof.text:
For this Borel, use the root subgroups of [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations]. By [lem-sfb-maximal-torus-overgroup-root-generation], $\gamma\in\Phi_P$ exactly when $U_\gamma\subseteq P$. In particular $\Phi^+\subseteq\Phi_P$. A representative $n$ of $w\in W$ conjugates $U_\gamma$ to $U_{w\gamma}$: conjugation gives a smooth connected $T$-normalized subgroup with that tangent character, so the uniqueness assertion for root subgroups applies. For any positive root $\beta$, we claim
$$s_\beta\text{ has a representative in }P(F)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad-\beta\in\Phi_P.$$
The forward implication follows by conjugating $U_\beta\subseteq B\subseteq P$. For the reverse implication, [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections] supplies the reductive rank-one centralizer $G_\beta$ through $T$. In each of its three matrix models in [lem-sfb-split-rank-one-classification], the two off-diagonal unipotent subgroups identify with $U_\beta,U_{-\beta}$ by their tangent characters and root-subgroup uniqueness. Their elements
$$\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$$
(or their images in $\operatorname{PGL}_2$) give the nonidentity rank-one normalizer class, namely $s_\beta$. All factors lie in $P(F)$. This calculation also holds in characteristic two.

source.place: Theorem 21.91, printed p.454, rank-one subgroup step; 21.66, p.444; rank-one models of Theorem 20.33, pp.419--420.

proof.text: Put $I=\{\alpha\in\Delta:-\alpha\in\Phi_P\}$, let $W_I\subseteq W$ be the subgroup generated by the $s_\alpha$ with $\alpha\in I$, and let $W_P$ be the image of $N_G(T)(F)\cap P(F)$ in $W$. It is a subgroup, since $T(F)\subseteq P(F)$. The preceding step shows that $s_\alpha\in W_P$ exactly when $\alpha\in I$; thus $W_I\subseteq W_P$. Conversely take $w\in W_P$ and a reduced expression $w=s_{\alpha_1}\cdots s_{\alpha_m}$, whose existence is supplied by [lem-sfb-bruhat-simple-letter-specialization]. A representative $n_w\in P(F)$ has $B(F)n_wB(F)\subseteq P(F)$ because $B\subseteq P$. Since $P$ is closed in $G$, the same node places every $n_{s_{\alpha_j}}$ in $P(F)$. The equivalence in the preceding step gives $\alpha_j\in I$ for every $j$, so $w\in W_I$. We have proved $W_P=W_I$, including the identity with its empty word.

source.place: Theorem 21.91, printed pp.453--454, exhaustion via the Weyl cells; the reduced-word specialization makes explicit the subgroup-exhaustion step.

proof.text: Suppose $-\beta\in\Phi_P$ for a positive root $\beta$. Step 3 gives $s_\beta\in W_P=W_I$. Each generator $s_\alpha$, $\alpha\in I$, acts as the identity modulo $\mathbf Q I\subseteq X\otimes\mathbf Q$, since by [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections] the Weyl element $s_\alpha$ acts on $X$ by $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$, where this coroot is that of [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure], by the uniqueness there of the cocharacter satisfying the reflection identity. Hence $s_\beta(\beta)-\beta=-2\beta$ belongs to $\mathbf Q I$. Thus $\beta\in\mathbf Q I$. Its integer simple-root coordinates vanish outside $I$, by linear independence of $\Delta$, so $\beta\in\mathbf Z I$, and also $-\beta\in\mathbf Z I$. Positive roots already lie in $\Phi_P$, so this proves $\Phi_P\subseteq\Phi^+\cup(\Phi\cap\mathbf Z I)$. All this calculation takes place in the rational character space, independently of $\operatorname{char}F$.

source.place: The root-set identification after Theorem 21.91 and Proposition 21.90; elementary reflection formula and base-coordinate calculation.

proof.text: In the rational root space $V=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbf Q}\Phi$, the coroot functionals and reflections give the reduced crystallographic system of [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]; its simple-root base is $\Delta$, which spans $V$ since it is independent and every root is an integral combination of it; reducedness $\Phi\cap\mathbf Q\alpha=\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$ is [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections]. By that node the Weyl elements $s_\alpha$ act on $V$ by these reflections, so the subgroup $W_I$ of Step 4 maps onto the reflection group $W_I$ of the orbit node, and $n\in N_G(T)(F)$ representing $w$ acts on characters by the action used in Step 3. If $\gamma\in\Phi\cap\mathbf Z I$, [lem-sfb-root-subsystem-simple-orbits] gives $\gamma=w\alpha$ for some $\alpha\in I$ and $w\in W_I$. By Step 4, $w\in W_P$, so choose a representative $n\in P(F)$. We have $U_\alpha\subseteq B\subseteq P$, and conjugation gives $U_\gamma=nU_\alpha n^{-1}\subseteq P$, using the root-subgroup uniqueness in [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations]. Apply [lem-sfb-maximal-torus-overgroup-root-generation] to conclude $\gamma\in\Phi_P$. Together with $\Phi^+\subseteq\Phi_P$, this is the reverse inclusion and proves the displayed equality.

source.place: Proposition 21.90 and Theorem 21.91, printed pp.453--454, subsystem roots; Appendix C.22, printed p.612, subsystem Weyl orbit.

proof.text: For any $J\subseteq\Delta$ satisfying the same equality, a simple $\alpha\in\Delta$ has $-\alpha\notin\Phi^+$ and belongs to $\mathbf Z J$ exactly when $\alpha\in J$, by independence of the simple roots. Consequently $J=\{\alpha\in\Delta:-\alpha\in\Phi_P\}=I$. This proves uniqueness and the stated equivalent formula for every allowed $B$. If $\Phi=\varnothing$, then $\Delta=I=\varnothing$ and the equality is empty; if $P=G$, then $I=\Delta$. No step required semisimplicity, simply connectedness, or a bound on the characteristic.

source.place: The uniqueness clause of Theorem 21.91, printed p.453; elementary simple-root coordinates.

proof_origin.place: Theorems 17.10, 17.16 and 21.91, Proposition 21.90, with a reduced-word proof of exhaustion and explicit root-set calculation. The two auxiliary inputs are left as statement-only nodes.
